content: The intended audience for this guideline includes the following groups: 1. National policymakers within health ministries who are responsible for shaping health-related policies. 2. Program managers involved in child health, essential drug distribution, and health worker training programs. 3. Healthcare providers, researchers, and clinicians who deliver services to pregnant women and mothers living with HIV at various levels of healthcare. 4. Development partners offering financial and/or technical support for child health programs, including those operating in conflict and emergency settings. The guideline was developed using evidence-informed recommendations, following the procedures outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The process involved several steps: Identifying priority questions and outcomes. Retrieving relevant evidence. Assessing and synthesizing the evidence. Formulating recommendations, including identifying research priorities. Planning for dissemination, implementation, equity, and ethical considerations. Evaluating the impact and updating the guideline as necessary. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) method was employed to prepare evidence profiles based on systematic reviews of preselected topics. In November 2014, the WHO Guideline Development Group reviewed the previous guidelines on HIV and infant feeding, identifying specific questions for updates. These updates primarily focused on one recommendation (number 2) from the 2010 WHO guidelines, while all other recommendations and principles remained valid. Four key areas were prioritized for review: 1. The duration of breastfeeding by mothers living with HIV. 2. Interventions to support infant feeding practices among mothers living with HIV. 3. Guidance for situations where mothers living with HIV do not exclusively breastfeed (e.g., whether mixed feeding with antiretroviral therapy (ART) is better than no breastfeeding at all). 4. Guidance for mothers living with HIV who do not plan to breastfeed for 12 months (e.g., whether shorter planned breastfeeding durations with ART are better than no breastfeeding at all). The Guideline Development Group also examined the implications of these recommendations in two programmatic areas: Guidance on infant feeding for mothers living with HIV and health authorities in conflict or emergency settings. Implications of the updated recommendations for monitoring and evaluation. To develop these recommendations, a WHO Steering Committee and a Guideline Development Group of 21 experts were convened. Based on evidence reviews, the Steering Committee drafted initial recommendations, which were then reviewed and finalized by the Guideline Development Group using the GRADE method. The finalized recommendations and guiding practice statements were submitted for approval to the WHO Guideline Review Committee. WHO commissioned independent institutions to conduct systematic reviews of the identified questions. Experts provided technical support by preparing systematic reviews, developing additional models, and drafting evidence summaries and GRADE tables. Members of the Guideline Development Group declared relevant interests, but none were deemed to represent a conflict of interest. This updated guideline does not encompass all WHO recommendations related to HIV and infant feeding but focuses on areas prioritized for updating. The recommendations from the 2010 WHO guidelines remain valid except as noted. Specifically, recommendation 2 from 2010 has been revised regarding the duration of breastfeeding, as reflected in recommendation 1 in 2016. Additionally, a new area of guidance has been introduced (recommendation 2 in 2016). The 2016 WHO recommendations on HIV and infant feeding include the following: 1. Mothers living with HIV should breastfeed for at least 12 months and may continue breastfeeding for up to 24 months or longer, similar to the general population, while being fully supported for ART adherence. This recommendation updates the 2010 guidance on breastfeeding duration. Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first six months, followed by continued breastfeeding with appropriate complementary foods introduced at six months. 2. Facilityand community-based interventions can improve the quality of infant feeding practices among mothers living with HIV. These interventions are strongly recommended based on high-quality evidence. Guiding practice statements address specific challenges: If a mother living with HIV does not exclusively breastfeed, mixed feeding with ART is better than no breastfeeding at all. ART reduces the risk of postnatal HIV transmission in the context of mixed feeding. If a mother living with HIV plans to return to work or school and does not plan to breastfeed for 12 months, shorter durations of breastfeeding with ART are better than never initiating breastfeeding. Countries are encouraged to hold discussions with key stakeholders to inform decision-making on implementing these recommendations into national programs. The guideline will be reviewed in 2019, with updates made as needed based on new evidence. The overall purpose of this guideline is to improve the HIV-free survival of HIV-exposed infants by providing guidance on appropriate infant feeding practices and the use of antiretroviral drugs for mothers living with HIV. It also aims to update WHO-related tools and training materials. The guideline addresses four aspects of infant feeding in the context of HIV: 1. The duration of breastfeeding by mothers living with HIV. 2. Interventions to support infant feeding practices by mothers living with HIV. 3. Guidance for situations where mothers living with HIV do not exclusively breastfeed. 4. Guidance for mothers living with HIV who do not plan to breastfeed for 12 months. The guideline informs national policymakers, program managers, healthcare providers, researchers, and clinicians involved in managing pregnant women and mothers living with HIV. It also updates development partners providing financial and technical support for maternal, newborn, and child health programs. The 2010 WHO principles and recommendations on HIV and infant feeding remain valid except as noted. These principles include balancing HIV prevention with protection from other causes of child mortality, integrating HIV interventions into maternal and child health services, and setting national or subnational recommendations for infant feeding in the context of HIV.
